question: Is it haram for Muslims to participate in protests?
asked: Shaykh, you recently participated in a protest against Modi's visit, and I commented positively about it in a gathering I was in. Then somebody showed me a fatwa from a well-known shaykh saying that participating in protests is haram and un-Islamic. Now I'm confused. What is the response to this?
answer:
So this is the question: there is a very famous shaykh, one of the grand shaykhs of another country, very well known in that movement, and he basically said that Muslims should not participate in protests. It is haram, and therefore he is saying it is a sin.

Now, I took on this question because, look, I get bombarded with a lot of questions. I have to choose questions that I feel are more beneficial than just the questions themselves. The previous one, I felt it opened up a door to interesting aspects of theology. This one opens up an interesting aspect of methodology.

And this is as follows. One of the positions that I have been advocating for many, many years is that **Muslims in any community should always take their fatwa from scholars who live in their own communities.** This is something I have been advocating ever since I studied overseas and saw with my own eyes how culture plays a role on knowledge. Because we are all human beings, all of us. Even the greatest 'alim is, at the end of the day, a human who is impacted by his or her culture. And if you just want to see this, I can give you so many examples from my own life, seeing how various ulama have interpreted various things. This is not disrespectful to those ulama at all. On the contrary, it is humanizing them, and it is respecting our local clergy and ulama.

And there are many examples. Perhaps the most cliched one, perhaps the most classic one, is that of Ibn Taymiyyah and the Mongol invaders. The Mongols, as you know, had nominally accepted Islam. They claimed to be Muslim. And Ibn Taymiyyah did not view them as being mainstream Muslims, because their beliefs were very bizarre, but they said, "We are Muslims."

And you know the famous story, it's a very famous story, that the Mongols invaded Damascus and took over aspects of the city, and they were very far from Islam. And as you know, they are soldiers, so they're going to be looting and plundering and raping, what soldiers do. So Ibn Taymiyyah and his students passed by a group of Mongol soldiers who were lying there drinking alcohol, semi-drunk. They were lying on their couches and whatnot on the street, and they were just drinking khamr in public, in a Muslim land. I mean, this is munkar. Of course people drank alcohol back then, but there's some haya: go do it quietly, don't get drunk in the streets. Here these soldiers were publicly with bottles and liquor and whatnot, drinking in the streets.

Ibn Taymiyyah's students said, "Let's go and advise them to fear Allah and give up alcohol." Ibn Taymiyyah said, "No, let them drink. Let them drink, let them go get more drunk." The students said, "These are Muslims, they claim to be Muslim. How can you allow this munkar to be public?"

Now let me pause here. Imagine if anybody had said, "Shaykh, so-and-so in a faraway land, we have an 'alim who publicly allows other Muslims to drink alcohol. What is the verdict on that 'alim?" You see, it's so easy to take a scenario, cut and paste, and go feed it to a mufti 5,000 miles away. The same mufti who claims to be among Ibn Taymiyyah's followers would have said Ibn Taymiyyah is a mubtadi', or whatever he would have said. This is common. That's the way it is when you feed the shaykh half an image. What do you think is going to happen?

Ibn Taymiyyah said, "Let these people drink and get drunk." And the famous response: the students said, "Why?" Ibn Taymiyyah said, "These people, if they are sober, they plunder, steal, rape and kill other people, whereas when they're drunk, they're just lying on the streets harming nobody but themselves. Between the two, it is better that they stay drunk and only harm themselves."

See, this is what you call contextual fiqh. This is what you call taking into account the circumstance. And by the way, I'm not teaching anything; this is standard fiqh. Every faqih who is worth his knowledge of fiqh knows this, that you need to understand. Ibn al-Qayyim mentions that half of giving a fatwa is to know the context of the fatwa; half of giving the fatwa is to know the context of the people you are giving the fatwa amongst.

And it is a huge problem that I have seen first-hand, and any person who studies fiqh sees this. It is a problem when you outsource your knowledge to a mufti on another continent. It is a huge problem, because the circumstances are different, and so you will import something that is not applicable in the environment you are in. It is a problem for us to ask, and frankly it is a problem for the mufti to even respond. That's why if anybody comes to me and asks a question about another land, I say: go to the shaykhs of your own land, don't come to me. I'm not a person who knows your situation that well.

So this great 'alim of this great land gave a fatwa that is very famous, in which he said it is haram. By the way, subhanAllah, haram is such a big word. You know what haram means? Haram means you're potentially going to be punished, that Allah will punish you. And I have to say as well, sometimes it's so common for people to use this word as if it means nothing. Haram itself should come with a warning label: only used in extreme cases. Haram means you are saying that Allah will potentially throw somebody in Jahannam and punish somebody.

By what evidence do you say that protests are haram? You read his fatwa, and he gives very generic evidences. Of them is that the ruler should not be opposed, khuruj, and this and that. Very generic fatawa. And here, subhanAllah, again you just wonder at the things he says. By the way, I'm not inventing this; this is in his fatwa. He says that protests are a form of chaos, and protests are unbecoming of the dignity of a Muslim. This is what he says: protests, you are shouting in the streets; it is unbecoming of the dignity of a Muslim to go and participate in a protest. So he brings forth a lot of various things together with the fatwa, and he says it is haram in any part of the globe to do any protest.

And again, with respect to the personality of this shaykh, I say that I'm not speaking about his culture. Even though, by the way, we get to the deeper issue of a fatwa that is very politically convenient for the kingdoms and the kings and the rulers of those lands, and that's a whole different topic that we're not going to get into. But see, human beings are human beings, and a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah. But be careful when a fatwa is given by an authority. And anyway, you get the point here. There's a self-serving issue; one needs to be careful. Look at the spectrum of positions, even from that society. Generally speaking, the establishment gives one fatwa, and those outside the establishment give another fatwa. You've got to scratch your head and wonder what's going on here. So be a little bit more critical.

And it is sad, the reality we live in, but that's one of the reasons why our ulama of the past were very careful where their income came from. It's because they didn't want anybody to doubt their fatawa and their knowledge. And unfortunately things have changed, and it's a very sad reality. But our classical ulama, our early ulama, generally speaking, did not want to work for a government that would impede their fatawa. And that's why the greatest ulama... Abu Hanifa was offered the position by the khalifa. Abu Hanifa refused: "I'm not going to be the qadi under you. I don't want to be that." He didn't want his knowledge to be impugned. Imam al-Bukhari was offered a government salary. None of them wanted it; they did not like this, because they were worried. And it's not just a matter of... maybe your own nafs gets involved, maybe you don't even know, and it's subconscious.

So my point is: just take this with a grain of salt. Look, let's just be fair and say, okay, this is one opinion of one shaykh, but that doesn't necessarily apply in any other context. In this culture that we live in, in American culture, protests mean something very different than in this shaykh's culture.

In fact, what a protest does is draw public attention. People who are unaware of a problem become aware of a problem. People who are unaware of how severe an issue is, that is brought to their attention. And all you need to do is look at some of the effects that protests have had in recent history.

Of the most important, cataclysmic changes that have taken place is the civil rights movement. The entire country changed, and the laws of the country changed, based on what? Beginning with what? Public protests in Birmingham, Alabama, when the dogs were sent out, when fire hoses were used. People saw this is inhumane. People who were on the fence were no longer on the fence. Politicians realized: we cannot continue this way. So protests played a primary role in changing the psyche of a culture. If they had sat home and said, "Oh, whatever, protests are haram," do you think anything would have happened? I mean, Allah, sometimes you just wonder.

Not just this; so many things, even movements we don't necessarily agree with: feminism and the feminist movement. All of these changes began with protests, and the right to whatever they wanted to do. It was protests. Other movements and strands which we don't necessarily agree with: again, it was protests that caused that change to happen.

Even political changes: India and the British occupation of India. As we all know, there were peaceful protests led by Gandhi and also by Jinnah, because at that time, remember, Jinnah and Gandhi did cooperate and collaborate to some level in these protests. And as you know, the whole notion of a free India, of throwing the yoke of colonialism off, right? The non-violent protests of Gandhi, beginning with the Salt March back in, what, 1928, whatever it was. So my point is that it literally changed the course of history. If somebody had told the Muslims of India and the Hindus of India that it was haram, sit and let the British do whatever they're doing... SubhanAllah, you just wonder. That's a cultural fatwa. It's not a fatwa from Allah and His Messenger. It's a fatwa that, okay, in the best-case scenario, we say it's culture-relevant. In the worst-case scenario, we say there might be other... Anyway, let's not be too explicit about that.

My point being: there is nothing explicit in the Qur'an and Sunnah where Allah says do not engage in protests. Come on, there's nothing like this. On the contrary, if you look at Islamic history and you read Islamic history, you actually find protests did occur many times, especially when things became too difficult for people to bear. A number of times in Islamic history, when the price of basic food and drink became too much, there were protests on the street.

Another famous example: when Jerusalem was captured by the Crusaders and the khalifa did nothing in Baghdad, the Muslims went to the streets and the Muslims protested. Unfortunately it became violent, because they destroyed some of the property of the khalifa. But attention was drawn: how can you sit in your palace? How can you do this when the Crusaders have taken over Jerusalem? So the point is that even in classical history...

In fact, some ulama have even said (and I don't disagree with this, by the way; even though I don't necessarily agree, I don't disagree) that Aisha radiyallahu 'anha, and Talha and Zubayr radiyallahu 'anhum, what did they do when they gathered people and exited from Madinah? It was to draw attention to the killers of Uthman and the fact that they were still roaming the streets. Because again, the whole issue of the Battle of the Camel: remember, the Battle of the Camel was not intended to be a battle. Aisha radiyallahu 'anha did not leave with a sword; she left with a crowd, and the point was to protest: how can you not capture the qatalah, the murderers? And Ali had his own views. What was the point of tens of thousands of people coming and gathering more and more momentum and crowd? In the beginning it was not intended to be a war. It was intended as what? It was a type of protest. And I see this to be something that is very much an acceptable interpretation.

So the bottom line, my dear, dear brothers and sisters: contextualize your ulama. Don't raise me or any 'alim above... I'm not calling myself an 'alim, I'm a student of knowledge, but don't raise any of us above our level. We're all human beings, all of us. And if a shaykh that you respect immensely gives a fatwa, that's one shaykh. Look at other scholars as well. Don't do it yourself, but look at the community of ulama, and especially look at ulama who are living in your lands, understanding your pros and cons.

And honestly, I don't know of any 'alim who is effective in this land who is saying that protests are haram. I mean, honestly, it's nonsensical to say this. And the protest that we did in Houston was covered by international media. A lot of Americans are clueless that people are angry at Modi, people are angry about Kashmir. You know this; a lot of people are clueless. I participated, we participated, and the Houston Chronicle, CNN, many mainstream media, they said, "Oh, 10,000 people are protesting Modi. And look at them: they're Muslim, they're Hindu, they're Sikh, they're all coming together. Why?" Interviewing people: Kashmir, Kashmir, Kashmir. What has happened? Non-Muslims who have no clue are now being made aware, and this is the beginning of change.

Now, to be brutally honest, I'm not saying protests are the be-all and end-all. On the contrary, protests are one small thing that we should do. I am not a big fan of making this the main part of Islam, and that's why that's not my forte. That's not what I really want to do; it's not something I'm so eager about. But at the same time, it is one thing that we can do, and I did not have any problem going, and if need be, I will go again.

Now, what's the bottom line? Protests are not intrinsically haram. Are they necessarily permissible or mustahabb? It's case by case. And in all likelihood, even in these case-by-case scenarios, you're going to find a spectrum. You're going to find some ulama who say in this case it is positive, and some ulama who say in this case it is negative. Listen to the ulama of the local region and see what they say.

In North America, generally speaking, we have the law on our side. I'm not speaking about Egypt or Syria (hindsight is 2020); I'm talking to North America. When the founding fathers of this country kicked the British out, they bitterly resented the fact that the British prohibited them from complaining against the king. They bitterly protested: how come we cannot even petition our grievances? Because the king had said you can't even protest on the street. That is why in the constitution they enshrined the right of the people to protest against the government.

Context: the founding fathers had a context. Everybody has a context, right? The founding fathers of this country felt: this isn't fair, we can't even petition the government for change. So when they founded the constitution of this country, in the articles of the constitution, as all of us in this audience should know, they have that the government can never ban protests in totality. The most the government can do is to regulate where and whatnot, but the peaceful protest is enshrined in our constitution.

So for any shaykh of another land or country, where the king's royal decree says you should not protest, and he gives a fatwa that protests are haram: please spare me. That's one land. In this country, no such fatwa should ever exist. Now, whether a particular protest is better or not is case by case, but **the default is that protests are mubah: neither are they wajib, nor are they haram.** And Allah knows best.
